title: Big-Button Corded Phones for the Kitchen or Bedside: Louder Calls and One-Touch Dialing
subtitle: How amplified, big-button landline phones work, what they cannot do, and how to choose one that fits your home and your hearing.
excerpt: A big-button corded phone puts bold numbers, one-touch calling and a louder handset where you need them most. Here is what to check before you buy.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: For many people, the phone on the kitchen wall or the nightstand is still the one they reach for first. It sits in the same spot, and you do not have to hunt for it. But an ordinary phone can have tiny buttons, a quiet ringer and a handset that makes voices sound far away.

Big-button corded phones are built to ease those everyday frustrations. They put large, easy-to-read numbers under your fingers, let you call family with one press, and some can make voices much louder than a standard phone. Here is how they work, what to check before buying, and three models to consider. Stock and prices change, so check the maker's site before you plan around any of them.
These are corded phones, meaning the handset is attached to the base by a curly cord. They plug into a phone jack like any landline phone. What sets them apart are a few helpful extras.

One-touch memory buttons let you store a number, such as a son's cell or the doctor's office, so a single press dials it. Some models have photo buttons, where a picture of the person sits on the button.

Amplification makes the caller's voice louder. It is measured in decibels (dB), a unit of loudness. The Serene Innovations HD-40P lists amplification up to 26 dB, the MaxiAids phone lists 40 dB of handset volume, and the HD-60 lists up to 55+ dB. Loud ringers and flashing lights help you notice a call from across the room.
Hearing aid compatibility matters too. The FCC says compatible handsets should reduce unwanted noise and work with the telecoil, a feature found in many hearing aids. The FCC consumer guide states:
"Telephones that are connected to traditional wireline telephone service must be hearing aid compatible." (FCC consumer guide, Hearing Aid Compatibility for Wireline Telephones and Wireless Handsets)

Only one of the phones below, the MaxiAids model, lists a dedicated 911 key. It is a handy shortcut, but all it does is place a phone call. It is not a monitored medical alert, and no phone can detect a fall or wandering. If that is a concern, a separate medical alert device is the better tool.

One more limit: a corded phone needs a working landline or landline-style phone service. If your phone service runs through the internet, the phone will not work during an internet outage unless that service has its own backup. And it will not help anyone who needs to make calls away from home.

items: Your phone service: The HD-40P needs an analog line, the traditional kind. If you have DSL internet on the same line, the maker says a DSL filter is needed to avoid static or dial-tone trouble.
Power: Some phones run entirely from the phone line or phone jack, with no outlet needed. Others need a wall adapter and offer battery backup. Check whether batteries are included.
A 911 key: If you want one, confirm it on the product page. Among the phones below, only the MaxiAids model lists one.
The right volume: Check the amplification range on the product page. For hearing concerns, or to decide how much boost you need, talk with your doctor or an audiologist (a hearing specialist).
Buttons and screen: Look for bold numbers, a backlit keypad if lighting is dim, photo buttons, and a caller ID screen with adjustable brightness.
Wall or desk: The HD-60 and the MaxiAids phone can be mounted on a wall, which keeps a kitchen counter clear.
Returns and stock: Check the return policy and confirm the phone is in stock.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well

Setup is usually simple: plug the phone cord into the wall jack and, if the model needs one, plug in the power adapter. If the phone has battery backup, put the batteries in on day one so they are ready when the power goes out.

Next, program the memory buttons together. Put the most-called people first and label each button clearly, with a photo if the phone allows it. Then try the ringer at each setting so it can be heard from the next room without being startling.

Amplified phones can be too loud for others in the house. If the phone has an auto-amplify switch, which turns the boost on with every call, the product pages recommend switching it off when others use the phone.

Check the maker's site for current stock and price before you plan around any of these phones. The Serene Innovations pages showed both models as sold out in November 2026, and no price was available for the MaxiAids phone. The HD-60 works only as a plain phone during a power cut, with no amplification, unless batteries are installed.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A good big-button phone will not do everything, but it can make the calls that matter easier to hear and easier to dial. Choose the features that fit, set it up together, and keep the numbers that count one press away.

products.name: Amplified Big Button Landline Phone With Photo Buttons (Model HD-40P)
products.price: $129.95 (price on maker's page, November 2026; shown as sold out)
products.blurb: Offers nine photo speed-dial buttons and amplification up to 26 dB. It runs on phone-line power, needs an analog line (a DSL filter is advised on DSL), and has no dedicated 911 key.

products.name: Amplified Phone for Hard of Hearing-Impaired Seniors (Model HD-60)
products.price: $149.95 (maker's site, November 2026; shown as sold out)
products.blurb: Offers amplification up to 55+ dB, a 95+ dB ringer with flashing lights and 12 one-touch memory buttons. It needs a 9 V wall adapter; 4 AA backup batteries (not included) give up to 4 hours of talk time, and without them it works as a plain phone in a power cut.

products.name: Big Button Caller ID Phone
products.blurb: Lists a preprogrammed 911 key, 40 dB handset volume, a two-way speakerphone and a caller ID screen. It runs from the phone jack alone, with no batteries or adapter.
